Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Ananya’s unraveling began on a rain-slicked service alley behind a closed grocery complex, where a man stepped from the shadows and gripped her wrist before she could react. He forced her to turn her back, commanded her to hand over her phone and delivery bag, and stood close enough that she felt entirely stripped of control. When patrol cars eventually squealed to a halt, their sirens and the officers’ barked commands only deepened her sense of suffocation, as if every authority figure in that moment replicated the original violation. Because the attacker had dictated her movements so completely, the mere sight of a police cruiser now sends Ananya’s attention snapping toward the officers inside; because the assailant had watched her with quiet predatory intent, a stranger lingering too long near a bike rack instantly registers as a threat. The traumatic night never settled into a coherent narrative but fractured into sharp snapshots: a frame of his scuffed boots, a frame of her trembling hands, a frame of the gray sky. Each time the rain hits her window, the auditory recall surfaces without warning—the exact rasp of his voice, the wet squeak of his soles—pulling the full emotional intensity of that event back into her chest. The memories that returned did not fade quietly. They reinforced her certainty that she could not stop bad things from happening to her, and they cemented her belief that she would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. Because she felt set apart from anyone who had not lived through that alley, her conviction of helplessness and isolation made every recalled moment feel sharper and more inescapable, pulling the emotional flood back with greater force. That intrusive recall flooded her with a sense of vulnerability so acute that she could not relax even when she knew she was in a safe place, forcing her to constantly identify escape routes before she felt comfortable anywhere. She began waking during the night to check whether she was safe, her hands automatically testing window locks and door handles as if preparing for another assault. Because she was always identifying escape routes and waking during the night to check whether she was safe, her nervous system stayed locked on high alert, which made the mere sight of a police cruiser or a person acting suspiciously immediately register as a trigger for loss of autonomy and perceived threat. This relentless state of threat directly pushed her toward numbing and withdrawal. Because the memory of the alley continued to trigger her inability to relax and her constant escape route planning, she found herself avoiding driving or being a passenger in a vehicle to quiet the dread, and she told herself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, clinging to magical thinking as a temporary shield. Because she felt helpless against the world and guilty about her frozen response, she turned to taking drugs to silence the panic, telling herself it was the only way to survive another day. Her decision to avoid driving fractured her work as a delivery driver; she started taking longer routes, missing drops, and ignoring app notifications, which led to a formal warning from her supervisor and a growing rift with her family, who mistook her withdrawal for indifference. As weeks turned into months, the cycle tightened with a weight that left little room for pause. The escape route planning and waking alert meant that she was always primed to notice a loss of autonomy or an authoritative voice, which immediately fed back into the auditory recall and the emotional flood of the mugging. That recalled intensity reinforced her negative appraisals of helplessness and isolation, which in turn made her unable to relax and compelled her to escape into drug use or avoidance. Avoiding control outside the car made every moment of forced action feel more suffocating, sharpening her sensitivity to authority presence and perceived threat. She had come to believe that safety was an illusion, and the magical thinking that once dampened her distress now left her hollow, stripped of the very agency she feared losing. What finally brought Ananya to seek help was a panic attack while loading packages onto her delivery bike, where the simple act of being instructed by a warehouse manager mirrored the original attack so precisely that she collapsed, trembling, on the asphalt. She is most afraid of losing her livelihood and drifting further into the isolation she has cultivated, but she is hoping to find a way to quiet the waking alert, reclaim the open road, and stop telling herself that the past never happened.
